children: By Todd Chanko

Faxes? According to Scott Berg, managing director of software research at Needham, many companies today still send invoices through this 20th-century technology. That fun fact means that after 29 years, there are still potential new customers for SPS Commerce.

The company provides supply-chain software to some 46,000 businesses, facilitating invoicing, revenue collection, and shipping for clients such as Burlington Stores, Walmart, and Amazon.com. Shares in Minneapolis-based SPS swooned in the so-called SaaSpocalypse, but they have nearly recovered all losses and are up about 50% since Feb. 25. Revenue grew 6% year over year in the second quarter, to $198 million, while non-GAAP earnings leapt 27% over the same period, to $1.27 per share.

It isn't just displacing faxes. SPS Commerce's rollout of agentic-AI tool MAX after a successful beta test, its own deployment of artificial intelligence to expedite onboarding, and a renewed strategic focus after divesting a recent acquisition could see its stock rise 30%.
Such catalysts haven't gone unnoticed: Earlier this month, Bloomberg News reported that private-equity firm GTCR was in discussions to acquire the company, though neither party would confirm.

"Investors should be interested in SPS Commerce because it is a vertically integrated cloud-based software company that is the dominant player in its field," says Berg. "Its scale and domain expertise make it very difficult for new entrants."

Deploying a combination of proprietary and commercial software, SPS Commerce manages the electronic data interchange and application programming interface communications for 750 million transactions annually across 33 million stock-keeping units, or SKUs. For example, instead of Home Depot facing thousands of differently formatted PDF invoices from thousands of suppliers, it mandates their use of SPS Commerce software.
A bonus for suppliers: Once on SPS Commerce's network, they have access to other retailers on the network. This is the "network effect" in action-a competitive moat that is hard to breach.

SPS Commerce's familiarity with the rules, policies, and procedures for each of its retailers and suppliers is extremely hard to replicate. This knowledge is both a source of revenue-its analytics segment generated $14.1 million, or 7.4% of the second quarter's recurring revenue-and a means of developing the MAX tool.

"We're able to train the agents on this proprietary database, and those agents are able to guide suppliers to execute their supply chain in compliance with their retail and distributor customers," Chad Collins, the company's CEO, said on its second-quarter call in July. "We look at trading patterns; we may see some differences in the way that Walmart or Target are handling some of their suppliers, see that at a macro level, and translate that into changes that the suppliers to those retailers need to make."

MAX was tested earlier this year by a limited number of customers. Many recovered revenue believed lost from supply-chain failures, such as miscoded invoices or underpayments, Collins said. One customer identified a $290,000 invoice error resulting from a bad UPC code; another discovered $70,000 in purchase orders.

"We're seeing customers identify different supply-chain anomalies using MAX through the chat feature," Collins said on the call. "They're able to get to some of those problems, get them resolved, resulting in hard ROI [return on investment] savings."
MAX was made available to all SPS Commerce customers earlier this month.

The company is also integrating AI into its own internal processes. "The top use case is going to be on the onboarding side," Joseph M. Del Preto, chief financial officer of SPS Commerce, said at Citigroup's Global TMT Conference earlier this month. "On average, that would take maybe a day or two for a person to help onboard that customer. The agent can do it in minutes." More rapid onboarding would not only increase customer satisfaction, but also have an immediate impact on revenue for customers and SPS Commerce alike. "The sooner we can onboard you, the sooner orders are flowing through, the sooner we can add more trading partners," Del Preto said at the conference.

SPS Commerce's January 2025 acquisition of Carbon6 hasn't met expectations, leading to the divesture of the third-party recovery business, announced in June. Carbon6's revenue derived from a portion of its Amazon third-party marketplace clients' recovered revenue. Amazon's change-requiring less inventory volume to meet its fulfillment standards-drastically altered Carbon6's revenue profile. Needham's Berg says the "jettisoning of Carbon6's [third party] revenue recovery unit" would remove the earnings overhang and reaccelerate SPS Commerce revenue growth as management realigns its core priorities.

Despite enviable relationships with suppliers and retailers, SPS Commerce could potentially be dislodged by new technologies. And a general economic slowdown crimping consumer spending could squeeze customers' margins, who then might clamor for price reductions. Lastly, although only 10% of its revenue is derived outside the U.S., continued geopolitical tensions could disrupt its overseas ambitions: The company hired a new European head last year, and is seeing promising results in the U.K. and Australia.

SPS Commerce has essentially no debt and generates a 20.7% free-cash-flow margin. Its shares offer a free-cash-flow yield of 6.7%; the company pays no dividends, but its share-repurchase program will potentially return about 5.2% to shareholders this year. The stock trades at 15.6 times forward earnings per share, well below the 47 times it traded in 2024.

A discounted cash-flow valuation with a terminal value of $3.06 billion, a working average cost of capital of 9.68%, and 5% free-cash-flow growth results in a target price of $121. A conservative expansion of its multiple to 18.7 times earnings, layered over an estimated 2026 $4.90 EPS, results in a target price of $91.60. Averaging these two methods yields a 12-month price target of $106, corresponding to a gain of about 30% over current levels.
Investors should send their broker an invoice for SPS Commerce shares.
